Overview: The American Tug 395 is a Lynn Senour-influenced raised-pilothouse semi-displacement cruiser built for efficient coastal passagemaking. It combines a single-diesel shaft layout, protected running gear, wide working decks and couple-oriented accommodations with substantially more beam and displacement than trailerable tug-style cruisers.

SoloHandling.Summary: Pilothouse visibility and accessible controls support short-handed operation.

More complex and costly to own than trailerable pocket cruisers

ModelVariations.Name: 34 / 365 naming evolution
ModelVariations.Description: American Tug describes the original platform as the 34/365. Historical 34 and later 365 naming overlap in the record; individual model-year documentation should control nomenclature.

ModelCharacter: The versatile middle American Tug: a 41'6" semi-displacement pilothouse cruiser offering one- or two-stateroom layouts and enough beam, tankage and machinery access for extended living without moving into the much larger 435/485 class.
DesignLineage: American Tug launched the 395 around 2010–2011 as a distinct model positioned between the 34/365 family and the larger 41/435.
The 395 broadened the brand's appeal with optional one- or two-stateroom arrangements and multiple power packages.
It retains the American Tug hallmarks of a Lynn Senour-influenced semi-displacement hull, raised pilothouse, wide side decks and single diesel.
The 395 is a distinct hull/model family, not simply a renamed 365.
OwnershipCharacter: A serious coastal cruising yacht that remains manageable for an experienced couple. Single-engine propulsion limits machinery duplication, but generator, thrusters, climate systems and substantial hotel loads are yacht-scale; future builder-specific support is uncertain because American Tugs entered Chapter 7 liquidation in July 2026.

Overview: The Grand Banks 36 Classic is a traditional tri-cabin flybridge cruiser with a semi-displacement hull, an aft owner cabin and a forward guest cabin. It was offered with single or twin diesel shaft propulsion and became one of the defining models of the Grand Banks range. Its layout provides substantially more privacy and cruising capacity than the 32 while retaining walkaround decks and lower and upper helm positions.

SoloHandling.Summary: Side decks and dual helms help, but the larger hull, windage and twin-cabin arrangement increase docking complexity.

Owners who value traditional Grand Banks layout and joinery

ModelVariations.Name: Long production evolution
ModelVariations.Description: Construction details, engines, tankage, interior arrangements and equipment changed during the four-decade production run.

ModelCharacter: The archetypal Grand Banks aft-cabin trawler and the model that established the brand's identity: two private cabins, wide walkaround decks, deep teak joinery and a semi-displacement hull designed to cruise efficiently yet tolerate more speed than a true displacement trawler.
DesignLineage: Grand Banks traces the Heritage series to the GB36, launched in the mid-1960s and one of the company's foundational designs.
Early 36 Classics were built in wood; fiberglass replaced wood construction in 1973.
The hull was enlarged late in the 1980s, adding roughly six inches of length and several inches of beam.
The 36 Europa and 36 Motor Yacht use the same underlying 36-family hull concept but substantially different deckhouse/aft-deck arrangements.
OwnershipCharacter: A highly serviceable cruising couple's boat, but old-boat condition dominates ownership cost. Teak decks and brightwork, aging tanks, windows, wiring and decades of owner modifications can make two apparently similar 36s very different propositions.
